details:
I like to go exploring. It's cool to find interesting random worlds not many people know about. However, sometimes you run into worlds that were not very well made--for example, they might be too poorly lit for my headset and eyesight (or for everyone's). In order to be able to see at all in those worlds, I want to include some sort of flashlight or other light source in my avatars.
This will immediately cause my avatars to be marked as "Poor" performance. Even though the light source in my avatar is toggleable, disabled by default. And, sure, I can understand how realtime lighting can multiply performance woes in a busy world. But there's a matter here of what the performance system is trying to accomplish and what it's actually accomplishing.
Let's see. I'm presented with a choice. I can either not include the light source and lose functionality that's important to me, or I can take the performance rating of "Poor" and assume that the vast majority of people will still see my avatar, and those who don't by default are more than well trained (by custom and circumstance) to unblock it. Since I'm not actually causing any performance degradation by including an inactive light, I have no moral qualms with choosing option A.
But now, here's the rub. My avatar has a "poor" rating, no matter how efficient it is in all of the other categories. What incentive do I have to make it performant (better than "Poor", at least), in any of them? Other than a sense of duty and willingness to make everyone's experience better, very little. It's hard work to make an avatar that's both good and performant. If I've already been punished in advance for poor performance, and any user of the avatar will be restricted anyway--it's only natural to assume that anyone who does see my "poor" avatar has accepted the risk of a "poor" performance avatar in the first place, since they have configured their client to show it--I'm much more incentivized to make an avatar that's cooler and more functional, even if it's less performant.
It wouldn't be so bad if this issue was specific to light sources, but no. That is far from the only perverse incentive in the system. The performance system has all the delicacy of a sledgehammer. All particle systems cost 2 material slots--regardless of whether they're actually used. But material source animations cost 0. All audio sources are treated equally, no matter how long, loud, high range or otherwise intrusive they are.
The v3 workflow of using menus and animations to control parameters of an avatar is directly at odds with the performance system, because it encourages--sometimes requires--the subdivision of the avatar into more meshes, more materials, etc. in order to permit their fine grained control... For toggles, there's the trick of putting the prop on a bone in the main avatar and scaling the bone down to 0, which I imagine is *less* performant than disabling the prop entirely, especially if the prop is complex (because the prop is still being rendered). For blendtrees, it turns out that animations can't control specific materials in a mesh, only every material at the same time, so instead of a mesh with multiple materials, I'm encouraged to have more meshes. 
I could use a custom shader to overcome this issue. But if I use a custom shader and the shader is blocked by the viewer's trust level, which is likely, the avatar might show incorrectly or broken. Sure, if the amount of meshes bumps the avatar into a worse performance rating, maybe the avatar won't show at all for a specific user. But if it does, it will show correctly, since I will be using standard shaders instead. And if the user can't see me at all--and a lot of others--they're much more incentivized to change things on their side in order to become capable of seeing us. If they see *something*, they have less of an incentive to do anything. And who wants to unblock shaders for everyone? The shaders some people use are way more obnoxious than any avatars marked poor performance but which don't necessarily perform that bad. By reasoning like this, I am, once again, incentivized to worsen my avatar's rating.
I want to suggest two key changes to the performance system in order to remove most of its perverse incentives and make it more sane for avatar makers to work with:
1. Make it point based. So for each category, "excellent", "good", etc. would be worth a certain amount of (polynomially increasing) points. Then add all the points together and use that value to determine the final performance rating of the avatar, using linear thresholds. It's not that complicated if the SDK control panel is doing all the work, and this means a single bad category doesn't entirely invalidate the performance optimization work of all the others. If certain categories are more important to you than others, just make them worth more points, but converselly account for the external incentives to use the thing in that category, too.
2. Dig deeper into components when determining the performance classification for each category. The system already does some digging in order to find how many materials are being used, etc. It would be nice it, for example, avatar makers were rewarded for objects that start inactive, or shorter and quieter audio.
title: [FEEDBACK] The perverse incentives in the performance/safety systems
